items.prompt: Differentiate between money capital and capital goods.
items.canonical_answer: Money capital is finance available to acquire productive resources, whereas capital goods are produced assets used to make goods or services.
marking_guidance: Comparison: finance available for purchases versus produced assets used in production; credit the paired distinction, up to two indicative practice marks.
This is an original indicative practice rubric, not a universal official mark-per-bullet rule.
items.provenance: Original Codex structural example; final subject is designated for Codex authorship and independent Claude Code review.

items.prompt: Suggest a useful purchase for an invented sewing group whose existing machine works but which has no cloth. Explain why this is preferable to buying another machine.
items.canonical_answer: Purchase cloth using available money capital. Cloth removes the stated input shortage so the working machine can be used; another machine would leave that shortage unresolved.
marking_guidance: Context: choose cloth to remove the specified missing-input constraint, using the existing working machine.
Reason: explain why another machine leaves that input shortage unresolved; three indicative practice marks across the choice and developed application.
This is an original indicative practice rubric, not a universal official mark-per-bullet rule.
items.provenance: Original Codex structural example; final subject is designated for Codex authorship and independent Claude Code review.

items.prompt: Explain the error in this statement: “An invented workshop’s N$600 cash balance and sewing machine are both capital goods.”
items.canonical_answer: The cash is money capital: it finances purchases. The machine is a capital good: a produced asset used in production. The distinction is whether the resource finances the productive activity or is equipment performing it.
marking_guidance: Error: cash is misclassified as a produced productive asset.
Distinction: cash finances production while the machine performs the productive task; up to two indicative practice marks.
This is an original indicative practice rubric, not a universal official mark-per-bullet rule.

items.prompt: State the two resource categories in this invented workshop: N$600 available cash and a working sewing machine [2]. Explain why buying cloth could be more useful than buying another machine when the workshop has no cloth [4].
items.canonical_answer: The cash is money capital and the machine is a capital good. Cloth is the missing input, so purchasing it allows the existing machine to produce bags. Another machine would not remove that shortage. This conclusion depends on the stated machine being usable; if it fails, equipment access becomes a separate priority.
marking_guidance: Point: identify cash as money capital and the sewing machine as a capital good; two indicative practice marks.

Development: explain the missing-cloth bottleneck, how buying cloth enables the working machine, why a second machine does not resolve it, and the dependence on the existing machine being usable; up to four indicative marks for the connected argument.
This is an original indicative practice rubric, not a universal official mark-per-bullet rule.
